source_text: Sit nunc, benedicti, carcer etiam Christianis molestus. Vocati sumus ad militiam dei vivi iam tunc, cum in sacramenti verba respondemus. Nemo miles ad bellum cum deliciis venit nec de cubiculo ad aciem procedit, sed de papilionibus expeditis et substrictis, ubi omnis duritia et inbonitas et insuavitas constitit. Etiam in pace labore et incommodis bellum pati iam ediscunt in armis deambulando, campum decurrendo, fossam moliendo, testudinem destinando, desudando. Sudore omnia constant, ne corpora atque animi expavescant de umbra ad solem et sole ad gelum, de tunica ad loricam, de silentio ad clamorem, de quiete ad tumultum. Proinde vos, benedicti, quodcunque hoc durum est, ad exercitationem virtutum animi et corporis deputate. Bonum agonem subituri estis, in quo agonothetes deus vivus est, xystarches spiritus sanctus, corona aeternitatis brabium angelicae substantiae, politia in caelis, gloria in saecula saeculorum. Itaque epistates vester Christus Iesus, qui vos spiritu unxit et ad hoc scamma produxit, voluit vos ante diem agonis ad duriorem tractationem a liberiore condicione seponere, ut vires corroborarentur in vobis. Nempe enim et athletae segregantur ad strietiorem disciplinam, ut robori aedificando vacent. Continentur a luxuria, a cibis laetioribus, a potu iocundiore, coguntur, cruciantur, fatigantur: quanto plus in exercitationibus laboraverint, tanto plus de victoria sperant. Et illi, inquit apostolus, ut coronam corruptibilem consequantur. Nos aeternam consecuturi carcerem nobis pro palaestra interpretamur, ut ad stadium tribunalis bene exercitati incommodis omnibus producamur, quia virtus duritia extruitur, mollitia vero destruitur.
thought_title: Prison as training ground for the contest
orientation: Tertullian continues addressing the imprisoned Christians, now reframing their hardship as military and athletic training for the coming contest of martyrdom.
pass_a_gloss: Let now, blessed ones, the prison be troublesome even to Christians. We were called to the military service of the living God already then, when we respond to the words of the oath. No soldier comes to war with luxuries, nor does he proceed from the bedroom to the battle line, but from tents that are ready and tightly girded, where all hardness and unpleasantness and discomfort has its place. Even in peace they already learn to endure war by labor and hardships, by walking about in arms, by running over the field, by digging the trench, by forming the tortoise formation, by sweating. All things stand firm by sweat, so that bodies and minds do not become terrified from shade to sun and from sun to frost, from tunic to breastplate, from silence to shouting, from rest to uproar. Therefore you, blessed ones, count whatever this hardship is as training of the virtues of mind and body. You are about to undergo a good contest, in which the judge of the contest is the living God, the trainer is the Holy Spirit, the crown of eternity is the prize of angelic substance, citizenship is in the heavens, glory is for ever and ever. Therefore your overseer Christ Jesus, who anointed you with the spirit and brought you out to this arena, wished to set you apart before the day of the contest from a freer condition to a harsher treatment, so that your strength might be built up in you. For indeed athletes also are set apart for stricter discipline, so that they may have leisure for building up their strength. They are kept from luxury, from richer foods, from more pleasant drink; they are compelled, tormented, wearied: the more they have labored in their exercises, the more they hope for victory. And those, says the apostle, do it to obtain a corruptible crown. We, who are about to obtain an eternal one, interpret the prison for ourselves as a training ground, so that we may be brought out to the stadium of the tribunal well trained in all hardships, because strength is built up by hardness, but is destroyed by softness.

choices.why: The Greek term denotes the official who presides over and judges an athletic contest; rendering it as a phrase preserves the technical sense for English readers.
The Greek term refers to the official who supervised athletes' training in the xystos; 'trainer' captures this role without importing modern athletic connotations.
The Greek term denotes one who stands over and directs; 'overseer' preserves the supervisory sense Tertullian applies to Christ.
The Greek term refers to the dug-up area where athletes competed; 'arena' conveys the place of contest without the wrestling-pit technicality.
Tertullian uses the military oath as a metaphor for baptismal commitment; 'oath' preserves the military and religious double sense.
The testudo is a specific Roman military formation with shields interlocked; the full phrase makes the military reference clear.

pass_b_english: But now, blessed ones, grant that even a prison is unpleasant for Christians. We were called to the military service of the living God at the very moment when we answered the words of the oath. No soldier comes to war with luxuries, nor does he advance to the battle line from his bedroom, but from tents that are light and tightly packed, where every hardship and discomfort and unpleasantness has its place. Even in peacetime soldiers learn to endure war through labor and troubles—marching under arms, running across the field, digging the trench, forming the tortoise formation, sweating it out. Everything is built on sweat, so that bodies and minds do not panic at the change from shade to sun, from sun to cold, from tunic to breastplate, from silence to shouting, from rest to uproar. Therefore, blessed ones, count whatever is harsh here as training for the strengths of mind and body. You are about to enter a good contest, in which the presider of the contest is the living God, the trainer is the Holy Spirit, the crown is eternity, the prize is angelic substance, citizenship is in the heavens, and glory is for ever and ever. And so your overseer Christ Jesus, who anointed you with the Spirit and brought you into this arena, wanted you to be set apart from a freer condition for harsher treatment before the day of the contest, so that your strength might be built up in you. For athletes too are separated off for stricter discipline, so that they can devote themselves to building up their strength. They are kept from luxury, from richer foods, from more pleasant drink; they are driven, tormented, exhausted. The more they have labored in their exercises, the more they hope for victory. And those men, says the apostle, do it to obtain a corruptible crown (1 Corinthians 9:25). We, who are going to obtain an eternal crown, interpret the prison as our training ground, so that we may be brought to the stadium of the tribunal well trained through every hardship, because strength is built by hardness, while softness destroys it.

problems.quote: the judge of the contest is the living God
problems.why: agonothetes is the presiding official of the contest, not specifically 'judge'; the glossary maps agon to 'contest' but the official title should reflect the presiding role, not a judicial one.
problems.fix: the presider of the contest is the living God
problems.ruling: agonothetes = contest official/director; translation 'judge' misrepresents role

problems.quote: We, who are going to obtain an eternal one, interpret the prison as our training ground
problems.source_quote: Nos aeternam consecuturi carcerem nobis pro palaestra interpretamur
problems.why: Latin specifies “eternal crown”; English drops “crown”, losing the object of the reward.
problems.fix: We, who are going to obtain an eternal crown, interpret the prison as our training ground
problems.ruling: Latin 'aeternam' (eternal crown) is implied from prior 'coronam'; English 'eternal one' preserves ellipsis but drops explicit 'crown' object.
